USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Proceed with the Section 301 tariff announcement tomorrow but frame it as leverage for negotiations, not as an opening salvo in a broad trade war. Target the tariffs narrowly at sectors tied to Made in China 2025 (tech, advanced manufacturing) while keeping the door open for Beijing to offer structural concessions on IP protection, JV requirements, and market access. Coordinate with EU and Japan who share US concerns on forced technology transfer.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is negative (opportunity-favorable) for the US at this moment. The US economy is in strong shape: industrial production at 102.2 and rising (country_health INDPRO), consumer sentiment at 101.4 — the highest in the lookback period (country_health UMCSENT), and unemployment low. The Fed is tightening gradually (FEDFUNDS 1.51%), signaling confidence. China's direct exposure to US steel tariffs is minimal — only ~2% of US steel imports come from China (NYT, Mar 3 2018) — so the Section 232 action is more about leverage than material economic impact. The Section 301 investigation has documented four categories of unreasonable Chinese practices: forced JV technology transfer, non-market licensing terms, state-directed IP acquisition, and cyber-enabled theft (USTR 301 Report, March 22 2018). This gives the US strong legal and moral standing. China has been cautious so far — Commerce Ministry expressed opposition but Liu He was in Washington seeking dialogue (NYT, Mar 3 2018). The risk of retaliation exists (Lighthizer acknowledged it on Capitol Hill, NPR Mar 21), particularly targeting US agriculture, but the US economy can absorb it better than China can absorb the tariffs. The action score is mildly toward escalation (-0.15) because the 301 tariffs are justified and necessary, but the US should not escalate beyond what the investigation supports. A negotiate posture is appropriate: the tariffs create leverage, but the goal should be structural Chinese reforms — not a trade war.
key_factors: Section 301 investigation completed with strong findings on IP theft and forced technology transfer
US economy is strong: industrial production rising, consumer sentiment at 101.4, low unemployment
China's direct steel exposure to US is only ~2% of imports — Section 232 is leverage, not substance
China has been cautious, signaling willingness to talk (Liu He visit to Washington)
EU and Japan share US concerns on forced technology transfer — coalition leverage available
White House set to announce ~$30-60B in China tariffs tomorrow (CNBC, Mar 21)
43 US trade groups oppose tariffs despite supporting IP goals — domestic political friction
China retaliation risk targets US agriculture — real but manageable
